content: Adrenergic drugs have been utilized in the management of urinary incontinence, but their clinical application has been limited due to concerns about their efficacy and potential side effects. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of adrenergic agonists in treating urinary incontinence in adults. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Trials Register as of September 15, 2010, and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving adults with urinary incontinence, where at least one arm of the trial included an adrenergic agonist drug. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted data according to the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. A total of 22 randomized trials met the inclusion criteria, 11 of which were crossover trials. These studies collectively involved 1,099 women, with 673 participants receiving an adrenergic drug. The specific adrenergic drugs studied included phenylpropanolamine (11 trials), midodrine (2 trials), norepinephrine (3 trials), clenbuterol (3 trials), terbutaline (1 trial), eskornade (1 trial), and Ro 115-1240 (1 trial). Notably, no trials included male participants. The limited evidence suggested that adrenergic agonists were more effective than placebo in reducing the frequency of incontinence episodes and the number of pad changes, as well as in improving subjective symptoms of urinary incontinence. In two small trials, adrenergic drugs appeared to be more effective than pelvic floor muscle training, although this finding may have been influenced by differences in treatment acceptability or withdrawal rates among participants. There was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of higher versus lower doses of adrenergic agonists or to compare their efficacy with estrogen therapy, whether used alone or in combination. Adverse effects were reported by over 25% of women using adrenergic drugs. The frequency of adverse effects was similar across groups receiving adrenergic drugs, placebo, or alternative drug treatments. However, side effects specifically associated with adrenergic stimulation, such as insomnia, restlessness, and vasomotor symptoms, were severe enough to lead to treatment discontinuation in approximately 4% of women. The authors concluded that there is weak evidence to support the use of adrenergic agonists over placebo for the treatment of urinary incontinence. The evidence is insufficient to assess their comparative or combined effects with other treatments. Larger, well-designed trials are needed to better define the role of adrenergic agonists in managing urinary incontinence. While most side effects were minor, some patients discontinued treatment due to these adverse effects. Rare but serious side effects, such as cardiac arrhythmias and hypertension, have also been reported.
